cues.text: A Long-Held Belief
The conviction that the Blessed Virgin Mary was preserved free from original sin from the very moment of her conception had deep roots.
It was expressed in the Church's liturgical and popular devotion, with feasts of the Conception of Mary celebrated in East and West for centuries.

Yet the precise theological status of the belief remained debated among medieval scholastics, with even figures such as St. Thomas Aquinas expressing hesitations later resolved in Mary's favor by Bl. John Duns Scotus's careful distinctions.
Growing Consensus
By the seventeenth century, popes such as Alexander VII had already affirmed the doctrine as among the truths revealed by God, even without a formal dogmatic definition.
Devotion to the Immaculate Conception flourished widely across the Catholic world, marked by countless churches, confraternities, and works of art dedicated under this title.
Pius IX's Definition
On December 8, 1854 , surrounded by a great assembly of cardinals and bishops in St. Peter's Basilica, Pope Pius IX promulgated Ineffabilis Deus .

The apostolic constitution solemnly defined that the Blessed Virgin Mary "in the first instance of her conception, by a singular privilege and grace granted by God, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Saviour of the human race, was preserved exempt from all stain of original sin."
What the Dogma Teaches
The definition applies specifically to the moment of the infusion of Mary's soul into her body in her mother's womb, not to the manner of her parents' conception.

It teaches that she alone among human beings, by a unique grace flowing from the future merits of Christ's redemption, never bore the stain of original sin inherited by the rest of humanity from Adam.
Confirmation at Lourdes
Catholics have long seen a striking confirmation of the newly defined dogma in the apparitions at Lourdes barely four years later, in 1858.
There, the visionary St. Bernadette Soubirous reported that the lady who appeared to her identified herself in the local Occitan dialect.
Her words were rendered in French as 'Que soy era Immaculada Councepciou' — 'I am the Immaculate Conception,' a title the young, unlettered peasant girl could not plausibly have invented herself.
Legacy

Ineffabilis Deus stands as one of the two occasions on which a pope has exercised the extraordinary charism of infallibility to define a Marian dogma, the other being the 1950 definition of the Assumption.

The definition further fueled Marian devotion across the Catholic world in the century that followed and remains a touchstone for Catholic teaching on grace, redemption, and Mary's unique role in salvation history.
